stance_basis: letter argues ORRVs must be classified individually, not grouped as a class, and supports ISIA position with additional emphasis on snowmobile distinctions
summary: Roger P. Worth, as Legal Counsel for Arctic Enterprises, Inc., submitted a comment letter supporting the ISIA's position while emphasizing that different types of ORRVs must be classified and regulated individually based on their distinct characteristics and environmental impacts. He argues that snowmobiles are fundamentally different from other ORRVs due to their winter-only use on snow, minimal permanent environmental impact, and reduced competition for land use, and that grouping all ORRVs together would contravene Executive Order 11644 and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963. He also calls for expanded, uniform safety performance standards developed in cooperation with industry.
complaint_summary: Worth argues on behalf of Arctic Enterprises that all ORRVs must be classified and regulated individually rather than as a single class, emphasizing that snowmobiles differ fundamentally from other ORRVs in their seasonal use, environmental impact, and land-use competition, and calls for expanded uniform safety standards developed with industry input.

statement.text:
The following comments are submitted on behalf of Arctic Enterprises, Inc., (Arctic) in response to the Notice of Availability of Draft Environmental Statement (Int Des 72-58) published in the Federal Register, Volume 37, No. 107 on June 2, 1972.
Arctic is the largest manufacturer of snowmobiles in the United States and second worldwide only to Bombardier, Ltd., the Canadian manufacturer of the Ski Doo and Motor Ski snowmobiles. Arctic also produces a line of mini-bikes, another type of off-road recreational vehicle (ORRV). Arctic produced over 110,000 snowmobiles during the 1972-73 snowmobile season.
Arctic firmly supports the position of the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) as set forth in the comments submitted on behalf of the ISIA by Patton, Boggs, Blow, Berill, Brand & May, as counsel for the ISIA. There are however, a few points that we believe need to be stressed.
Arctic believes that the various types of ORRV's <u>must</u> be classified and considered on an individual basis due to their differences in use, effects on other users of a particular area and the effects on the environment itself. A snowmobile travels over the temporary medium of snow. Underlying the snow is the <u>frozen</u>, dorment vegetation and ground. In contrast, other ORRV's travel over and can easily adversely affect the soft spongy ground, as in the Spring, and the growing plant life. In addition, during the winter months the areas are free of migratory birds and the hibernating animals.

Department of the Interior Page #2
June 28, 1972
Some ORRV's greatly damage the vegetation over which they travel and this damage is readily apparent to the eye while in most instances one cannot spot in summer the paths snowmobiles took the previous winter. While snowmobiles change the appearance of the landscape by leaving tracks in the snow, there is not sound evidence that there is any permanent adverse affects on the underlying vegetation. Snowmobilers have damaged seedlings and small shrubs, but we believe this is a matter that can be handled through education and restricting snowmobiles from those areas that are susceptible to such damage.
Arctic does not advocate the summer use of snowmobiles, since the vehicle is not designed for such use. If snowmobiles are fitted with wheels or otherwise modified for use on mediums other than on ice or snow, it is our position that they <u>must</u> be classified during those months of use with the other ORRV's that are similarly used and have similar effects.
Additionally, snowmobiles are used in the winter months when the competition for the use of any land area is at a minimum. Consequently, more areas should be open for snowmobiling in the winter than for an ORRV use during the other season.
Snowmobiles are not alone in the need for classification of ORRV's. Campers, for instance, should be allowed in certain areas where motorcycles and dunebuggies are prohibited for obvious reasons.
In order to insure safe use of snowmobiles on public lands, uniform safety performance standards must be developed and enforced. The current state standards are underdeveloped and inconsistent one with the other. The Department of Interior is the logical agency to work with the industry to develop meaningful standards since it will understand the vehicle, the conditions of its use and will be charged with the responsibility of controlling the enforcement of the snowmobile use and required safety equipment. The safety and machine operating requirements in the Draft Environmental Statement, are rudimentary and must be greatly expanded upon to insure safe operation on public lands.
8

To summarize, our position, all ORRV's cannot and must not be grouped together as a class. To do so would be to contravene the intent and the words of Executive Order 11644 and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963.
Very truly yours,
ARCTIC ENTERPRISES, INC.
Roger P. Worth Legal Counsel
